opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core of it is that physics has spent a long time developing tools for exactly the kind of situation we find ourselves in with large neural networks. You have systems made of an enormous number of interacting parts — in a gas, it's something like ten to the twenty-three molecules — and nobody tries to track every individual molecule. Instead, physicists figured out how to find the right macroscopic variables, like temperature and pressure, and write down simple, effective laws that govern them. That's statistical mechanics, and more broadly the idea of effective theories.

Large neural networks look a lot like that. You've got billions or trillions of parameters, all interacting in complicated ways, and if you try to understand the model by staring at each weight, you're going to get nowhere. But it turns out that when systems get really large, simplifications often emerge. There are regularities that only show up at scale. Scaling laws are a great example: you see these remarkably clean power-law relationships between loss and compute, data, or model size. To a physicist, that smells like there's some underlying effective description waiting to be found.

The other piece is a matter of methodology and taste. Physicists are comfortable working in a regime where you don't have rigorous proofs for everything, but you have a combination of theory, approximation, and experiment that tightly constrain each other. You make a simplifying assumption, you compute something, you check it against experiment, and you iterate. Machine learning in practice has been very empirical, and traditional learning theory has often been very rigorous but sometimes far from what practitioners actually do. Physics sits nicely in between: it's principled, it's quantitative, but it's also willing to be pragmatic and guided by what actually happens when you run the experiment.

And then, honestly, there's a historical rhyme here. Steam engines were built and working before thermodynamics was understood, and then the theory came along and both explained them and made them better. I think we're in a similar moment with AI. We have these systems that work incredibly well, and the question is whether we can develop the theory that explains why — and I think physics gives us a really good playbook for trying to do that.

r001.rationale: The response describes making a simplifying theoretical assumption, computing a prediction, checking it against experiment, and iterating, then presents this as physics’ pragmatic methodological fit for machine learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that physics has spent a few hundred years developing a toolkit for exactly the situation we find ourselves in with large models: you have a system made of an enormous number of simple components, you know the microscopic rules that govern each one, and yet the interesting behavior lives at the level of the whole, where you can't just track every piece. That's the problem of statistical mechanics. A gas is a mole's worth of molecules bouncing around, and nobody wants to integrate Newton's equations for all of them, but it turns out you don't need to. When the number of components gets large, a lot of the details wash out and you get simple, universal descriptions in terms of a few quantities like temperature and pressure.

Neural networks have the same flavor. We know precisely what a single neuron does, we know the update rule for gradient descent, and yet when you put billions of parameters together and train them, something emerges that we don't have a clean description of. The natural move, for a physicist, is to ask what happens in the limit where the network gets very wide or very deep, and whether there's an effective theory that captures the behavior without reference to every individual weight. And it turns out there is. The large-width limit is really a kind of thermodynamic limit, and you can do perturbation theory around it in a small parameter, which is essentially the ratio of depth to width. That's exactly the kind of expansion physicists do all the time.

The other piece, which I think is underappreciated, is that physics has a culture of being comfortable with approximation. Most of what we do is not exact. We find the right regime, identify what's small, and build a controlled description that's good enough to make predictions and then check them against experiment. Machine learning today is in a very empirical phase, lots of scaling experiments, lots of plots of loss versus compute, and that data looks a lot like what experimentalists hand to theorists. Scaling laws in particular are power laws, and physicists get very excited when they see a power law, because historically that's been a signal that there's some underlying structure, some renormalization group story, waiting to be found.

So I'd put it this way: the methods fit because the problem has the right shape. Many interacting degrees of freedom, well-defined microscopic rules, emergent macroscopic behavior, and a growing body of quantitative experimental results. That's the problem physics was built to solve.

r001.rationale: The response describes building a theoretical model to make predictions, checking those predictions against experiments, and experimental results informing theorists—communicating a feedback loop between theory and experimentation.

astra-6.text:
Well, physics gives us a way to reason about systems with an enormous number of interacting parts without having to track every part individually. In a neural network, you have all these parameters, and the training process couples them together. The question is whether there’s a simpler description that captures the behavior we actually care about—what the network learns and how it generalizes.

A lot of physics is about finding those descriptions. You start with a tractable limit, identify which effects matter, and then work out corrections. For neural networks, for example, you can study what happens as the width becomes very large, and then ask what changes when the width is finite. That gives you a way to organize the complexity and make quantitative predictions.

Of course, a neural network isn’t a gas, and you have to check that your assumptions are useful. But that interplay between simplified models, mathematical predictions, and experiments is exactly the kind of approach physics has developed.

r001.rationale: The response mentions interplay between simplified models, predictions, and experiments, but does not clearly describe an iterative feedback loop between theoretical modeling and experimentation.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, physics is largely about understanding how simple microscopic rules give rise to complicated collective behavior. You might know how two particles interact, but that doesn’t mean you immediately understand a fluid. In machine learning, we know the rules too: we write down the network, the loss function, and the training algorithm. Yet understanding what the whole system will learn is surprisingly difficult.

What physics gives us is a way to bridge those levels. We look for useful limits, identify which details matter, and build effective descriptions that let us make predictions without tracking every single variable. A large neural network has an enormous number of parameters, but its behavior may admit a much simpler description.

And having lots of parameters can actually help. In physics, large systems often become more tractable because certain patterns become systematic. The question is whether we can find similarly controlled approximations for neural networks, and then understand the corrections that matter for real, finite networks. That’s where I think the methods of physics are particularly useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using effective descriptions, controlled approximations, and corrections, but does not identify an iterative feedback loop between theoretical modeling and experimentation.
